newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura not missed on first day of suspension.
newsitem.headline: Nomura not missed on first day of suspension.

text.p: Investors were unfazed by the disappearance of scandal-hit Nomura Securities Co Ltd from the markets on Wednesday, but the exclusion of Japan's biggest broker could boost market volatility, analysts said.

"Even though Nomura was absent from trading, no major impact was evident at the Tokyo (stock) exchange. It wasn't the customers who were ordered to suspend stock transactions, so they could place orders through foreign and other Japanese brokers," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities.

Under orders from Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF), Nomura and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) suspended integral parts of their operations on Wednesday as punishment for making illegal payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.
The penalties against Nomura included a halt to stock and stock-related business at all branches from August 6 to August 12.
Market sources said Nomura's absence did not have any major impact on stock market activity on Wednesday.
The key Nikkei average closed 187.62 points higher at 19,702.07, with shares in both Nomura and DKB sharing in the gains. Nomura rose 50 yen to 1,680 yen, while DKB closed 70 yen higher at 1,520 yen.

But brokers said there was a chance that volatility could increase during Nomura's absence, as smaller brokerages, with fewer stocks on hand, would need to rely on margin transactions to handle large orders from investors.
"Market activity is thin as it is and if trading on margin increases, indices could move sharply," one broker said.

A strategist at a second-tier brokerage added: "Foreign investors or Japanese investors trading through foreign brokerages could take advantage of the thin trade to boost volatility in futures in order to obtain fast profits.
"Nomura's presence used to stem some of those moves in the past," he said.
Spokesmen at Nomura and DKB said they put up posters at branch offices detailing the penalties immediately after they were announced, and this helped keep confusion to a minimum.

"We have not heard of any major confusion at our branch counters," said a Nomura spokesman. "We cannot do any stock-related business at any of our offices for one week, but this could be a good opportunity to review our operations."
Nomura has about 135 domestic branches.

The spokesmen said that the firms would use the suspension period to work out a programme to improve internal supervision, as ordered by MOF. The ministry told the two to finalise a plan by September 19 for steps to prevent the recurrence of any payoff scandals.
The penalties, announced last week, were the harshest ever imposed in Japan for violations of securities or banking laws.
Nomura has also been ordered to halt stock dealing on its own account until the end of the year.

DKB was ordered to halt domestic lending to new customers except for housing loans until the year-end and to refrain from new overseas business except for lending. It was also banned from selling mutual funds at its branches and from making use of financial holding companies for a year.
DKB's 375 domestic offices have suspended lending to new customers, a DKB spokesman said.
Analysts said that the penalties against DKB would not hurt its bottom line significantly in the short term, as loan demand had slackened.
One analyst added, however, that there may be some negative impact on profits in the medium and longer term, due to an erosion of depositor confidence in the bank.
The impact of the penalties on Nomura's business results is expected to be severe for the current business year to next March, analysts said.
But they added that Nomura would probably avoid falling into the red in 1997/98.
"The penalties will hurt Nomura's bottom line in the current business year, but the company is unlikely to post a loss," said Kouya Hasegawa, a Nikko Research Center analyst.
For DKB, he said, the negative impact of the scandal may hinder growth at a time of "Big Bang" reforms to liberalise Japan's financial markets by 2001.
"In the banking sector, there are many domestic rivals to compete with DKB. But in the securities sector, Nomura doesn't have any major domestic rivals," Hasegawa said.

He also noted that Japanese media have reported that the other three of Japan's four big brokerages -- Nikko Securities Co Ltd, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd 8601 T and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd -- are suspected involvement in similar payoff scandals.
